evidence.claim: A short mountain crossing climbs above Whitesburg toward Oven Fork.
evidence.quote: this short byway travels over the 2,800-foot-high Pine Mountain and Little Shepherd Trail, from Whitesburg on US 119 to Oven Fork

evidence.claim: Pine Mountain Road carries US 119 over the ridge between Whitesburg and Oven Fork, crossing the Little Shepherd Trail along the way.
evidence.quote: this short byway travels over the 2,800-foot-high Pine Mountain and Little Shepherd Trail, from Whitesburg on US 119 to Oven Fork

evidence.claim: Kentucky designated this 8.153-mile road as a scenic byway in 1995.
evidence.quote: Beginning in Letcher County at the junction of US 119 and KY 15 in Whitesburg, via US 119 to the junction of US 119 and KY 806 near Oven Fork, a distance of 8.153 miles. 5/8/1995

evidence.claim: The National Scenic Byway Foundation promotes the mountain views along the crossing.
evidence.quote: Breathtaking views await as this short byway travels over the 2,800-foot-high Pine Mountain

evidence.claim: The ridge itself runs about 125 miles through Kentucky, Virginia and Tennessee, forming a long barrier to transportation.
evidence.quote: Pine Mountain is a ridge in the Appalachian Mountains running through Kentucky, Virginia and Tennessee. It extends about 125 miles (201 km)

evidence.claim: forming a long barrier to transportation.
evidence.quote: It has long been a barrier to transportation

evidence.claim: Only two waterways pass through the entire ridge: the Cumberland River at Pineville and the Clear Fork near Jellico, Tennessee.
evidence.quote: as the Cumberland River at Pineville, Kentucky is one of only two waterways that pass through the entire ridge. The other is the Clear Fork (Cumberland River tributary) near Jellico, Tennessee.

evidence.claim: The highway’s number changed as the national road network expanded.
evidence.quote: In 1934 US 119 was extended from Morgantown WV into Kentucky, joining US 123 at Jenkins; US 123 was then renumbered to US 119.

evidence.claim: The Pineville-to-Jenkins section became US 123 in 1930, then US 119 in 1934 when that route reached Kentucky.
evidence.quote: The following year this section was renumbered to U.S. Route 123, to allow US 23 to be extended in a different direction (towards Kingsport TN).  In 1934 US 119 was extended from Morgantown WV into Kentucky, joining US 123 at Jenkins; US 123 was then renumbered to US 119.

evidence.claim: The Pineville-to-Jenkins section became US 123 in 1930
evidence.quote: In 1929 U.S. Route 23, which then ended at Jenkins, KY, was extended to Pineville. The following year this section was renumbered to U.S. Route 123

evidence.claim: Kentucky’s US 119 originally connected Pineville, Cumberland and Whitesburg by a series of two-lane roads paralleling the mountain.
evidence.quote: Hwy 119 in Kentucky was originally a series of two-lane roads paralleling Pine Mountain that connected Pineville to Baxter (just north of Harlan) and then headed northeast through Cumberland, Whitesburg, and Pikeville

evidence.claim: Later work widened parts of the mountain crossing to make it safer for trucks.
evidence.quote: On the mountain, Hwy 119 has recently been widened in a number of places in order to make it safer for trucking traffic.

evidence.claim: Start at US 119 and KY 15 in Whitesburg, in the valley of the North Fork of the Kentucky River.
evidence.quote: Beginning in Letcher County at the junction of US 119 and KY 15 in Whitesburg, via US 119 to the junction of US 119 and KY 806 near Oven Fork, a distance of 8.153 miles.

evidence.claim: Whitesburg, in the valley of the North Fork of the Kentucky River.
evidence.quote: in the valley of the North Fork of the Kentucky River

evidence.claim: US 119 heads southwest over Pine Mountain, leaving the valley for the crossing.
evidence.quote: US 119 leads northeast 11 miles (18 km) to U.S. Route 23 at Jenkins and southwest over Pine Mountain

evidence.claim: After the Little Shepherd Trail, the byway continues to the US 119 junction with KY 806 near Oven Fork.
evidence.quote: Beginning in Letcher County at the junction of US 119 and KY 15 in Whitesburg, via US 119 to the junction of US 119 and KY 806 near Oven Fork, a distance of 8.153 miles.

evidence.claim: After the Little Shepherd Trail
evidence.quote: travels over the 2,800-foot-high Pine Mountain and Little Shepherd Trail, from Whitesburg on US 119 to Oven Fork

evidence.claim: Whitesburg occupies the valley of the North Fork of the Kentucky River, below the US 119 crossing of Pine Mountain.
evidence.quote: in the valley of the North Fork of the Kentucky River

evidence.claim: below the US 119 crossing of Pine Mountain.
evidence.quote: US 119 leads northeast 11 miles (18 km) to U.S. Route 23 at Jenkins and southwest over Pine Mountain

evidence.claim: The town began in 1842 on land Stephen Hiram Hogg offered for a county seat.
evidence.quote: Whitesburg was founded in 1842 on land offered by Stephen Hiram Hogg to build the county seat.

evidence.claim: First called Summit City, it was renamed for John D. White, who introduced the bill creating Letcher County.
evidence.quote: Previously called Summit city, it was renamed for John D. White who had introduced Letcher county's enactment bill in the State legislature.

evidence.claim: It remains the county seat.
evidence.quote: Whitesburg is a home rule-class city in and the county seat of Letcher County, Kentucky

evidence.claim: Here KY 15 meets US 119, which leads northeast toward Jenkins and southwest over the mountain toward Cumberland.
evidence.quote: It has its eastern terminus in the east part of Whitesburg at U.S. Route 119. US 119 leads northeast 11 miles (18 km) to U.S. Route 23 at Jenkins and southwest over Pine Mountain 20 miles (32 km) to Cumberland.

evidence.claim: The mountain crossing begins at that eastern end of KY 15; in the opposite direction, KY 15 connects Whitesburg with Hazard.
evidence.quote: Kentucky Route 15 passes through the city, leading northwest 31 miles (50 km) to Hazard. It has its eastern terminus in the east part of Whitesburg at U.S. Route 119.

evidence.claim: Oven Fork lies on US 119 south of Whitesburg.
evidence.quote: Oven Fork is located on U.S. Route 119 and the Cumberland River 4.2 miles (6.8 km) south of Whitesburg.

evidence.claim: Its name may have come from an oven used to fire bricks for local chimneys, or from German residents baking bread outdoors.
evidence.quote: The community may have got its name from a brick oven that produced bricks for the chimneys of the homes in the area. Or for Germans that lived in the area that baked bread in the open.

evidence.claim: The community’s first post office opened in 1879; a second opened in 1945 and closed in January 1993.
evidence.quote: The first of two post offices to serve the community was established on February 6, 1879

evidence.claim: a second opened in 1945 and closed in January 1993.
evidence.quote: The second Oven Fork Post Office was established in the spring of 1945, with Winnie Sumpter as its postmaster. It closed in January 1993.

evidence.claim: The scenic byway ends near the community at the junction of US 119 and KY 806.
evidence.quote: Beginning in Letcher County at the junction of US 119 and KY 15 in Whitesburg, via US 119 to the junction of US 119 and KY 806 near Oven Fork, a distance of 8.153 miles.

evidence.claim: Bad Branch Falls drops 60 feet over sandstone cliffs in a narrow gorge cut into Pine Mountain.
evidence.quote: The moderate 1.8 mile loop leading Bad Branch Gorge where the 60-foot waterfall flows over the sandstone cliffs

evidence.claim: in a narrow gorge cut into Pine Mountain.
evidence.quote: The deep and narrow gorge, adjacent to the Jefferson National Forest is carved into the face of Pine Mountain.

evidence.claim: Trails and footbridges pass through a forest of hemlocks and mixed hardwoods.
evidence.quote: Upon visiting, the trails and foot bridges will take visitors through a hemlock-mixed mesophytic forest.

evidence.claim: Tulip poplar, sweet birch, yellow birch and American beech grow with the hemlocks; flowering dogwood and rosebay rhododendron grow beneath the canopy.
evidence.quote: Tulip poplar, sweet birch, yellow birch, basswood, buckeye and American beech also grow alongside the hemlock species. Beneath the upper canopy of trees are the umbrella magnolia, sweet pepperbush, flowering dogwood, and rosebay rhododendron.

evidence.claim: The gorge’s shaded, moist conditions support rare species including painted trillium and Fraser’s sedge.
evidence.quote: The gorge creates the right conditions for a number of rare species that thrive in shaded, moist areas. Some of these species include the small enchanter's nightshade, Fraser's sedge, painted trillium

evidence.claim: The original protected area, including the waterfall, was dedicated as a nature preserve in September 1985.
evidence.quote: On September 26, 1985, the sold area, which included a 60-foot waterfall feature, was dedicated a nature preserve

evidence.claim: Sandstone boulders and cliffs accompany the gorge’s streams, with ridgelines and knobs providing views into the Appalachians.
evidence.quote: Sandstone boulders and cliffs along with riglines and knobs provide views into the Appalachia area. The terrain is landscaped with streams, rivers, and a 60-foot waterfall.

evidence.claim: The waterfall drops over sandstone cliffs.
evidence.quote: the 60-foot waterfall flows over the sandstone cliffs

flags: The official Kentucky record defines 8.153 miles from KY 15 to KY 806; material maps 43 miles from Harlan. Used the designated segment and reversed its strip order from Whitesburg to Oven Fork. Bad Branch remains a separate excursion after the crossing; no unsupported access directions supplied.

All current moments retained. Dropped the tagline’s unbounded claim that only two rivers ever crossed the ridge: the cache identifies two present waterways, not the complete geological past. Omitted the cached 1.8-mile waterfall-loop claim because the same article gives confusing 3-mile and 6-mile upper trail descriptions and lacks a current manager trail map.

The Oven Fork article calls the waterway the Cumberland River, while the Poor Fork article defines the mainstem beginning farther downstream. Omitted the exact waterway name at Oven Fork pending resolution.
Bad Branch history includes an anomalous 1900 acquisition date, an agency-name error (Nature Conservatory), and an undated only-pair-of-ravens claim; none reused.
The foundation’s 2,800-foot description concerns this crossing, not the entire ridge’s highest point. Avoided a precise summit elevation and its loosely described nearby resort park.
Oven Fork stays shorter because its naming evidence is uncertain and its documented place history is thin. Current story has no motifs field; story motifs default to an empty list.
